texts.facts: The said order was challenged by the accused - petitioner herein by filing Criminal Appeal before the learned Sessions Judge, Dahod, being Criminal Appeal No.50 of 2004, which came to be dismissed by the learned Sessions Judge, Dahod vide judgement and order dated 6/9/2005, thereby confirming the order of the learned trial court. 3.00. texts.arguments: 4.00. Mr.Y.V. Vaghela, learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner - accused has submitted that though the petitioner has some case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about sentence imposed by the courts below. He has, in this behalf, submitted that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act No. 34 of 1976, whereby sections 51 & 52 have been added and under the said section, only fine is leviable. Therefore, he has requested to maintain the conviction but impose reasonable fine in lieu of sentence imposed by the courts below. In support of his above submission, Mr.Vaghela, learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner accused has heavily relied upon the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court dated 17/3/2016 in the case of Nemi Chand Versus State of Rajasthan rendered in Criminal Appeal No.214 of 2016. 5.00. Mr.C.M. Shah, learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing on behalf of the State has requested to pass appropriate order considering the stand now taken by the petitioner - accused and the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemi Chand (supra). Narbhesing Parvatsing Rathod vs State Of Gujarat & on 22 September, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140766101/ 2 6.00. Having heard the learned advocates appearing on behalf of the respective parties and considering the facts of the present case, it is not in dispute that the petitioner has been convicted under section 16 of the Act and the Charge against the petitioner accused was only of sub-standardization HC-NIC Page 3 of 8 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:29:41 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/808/2005 JUDGMENT of milk. There was no allegation of any adulteration injurious to the health. Therefore, the case would squarely fall under sections 51 & 52 of the Central Amendment Act No. 34 of 1976. As observed hereinabove, the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner accused is not challenging the impugned judgement and order of conviction on merits and is, as such, giving up plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence imposed by the courts below. 6.01. Identical question came to be considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Nemi Chand (supra). While considering the aforesaid request, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as under :- "2. Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below. He has, in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was HC-NIC Page 4 of 8 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:29:41 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/808/2005 JUDGMENT added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable. He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in "T. Barai V. Henry Ah Hoe and Another" [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court. In the said judgment, the Court held as under :- "22. It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1). The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. But insofar as the Central Amendment Act reduces the punishment for an offence punishable under Section 16(1) Narbhesing Parvatsing Rathod vs State Of Gujarat & on 22 September, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/140766101/ 3 (a) of the Act, there is no reason why the accused should not have the benefit of such reduced punishment. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied HC-NIC Page 5 of 8 Created On Mon Oct 02 03:29:41 IST 2017 R/CR.RA/808/2005 JUDGMENT to mitigate the rigour of the law. The principle is based both on sound reason and common sense. This finds support in the following passage from Craies on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 388-89: A retrospective statute is different from an ex post facto statute. "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. They are certainly retrospective, and literally both concerning and after the facts committed. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction....
